title: Suffering belongs to the man, not the indwelling God
english: Then, showing plainly that the forms, that is, the sufferings, of splendor are attached to the man and not to the divine, he immediately brings in another quotation, adding: “A man in affliction, knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). So this is the one who, after his insults, was seen without appearance and without form, and then again from change clothed himself with splendor. For the God dwelling in him was not led to death like a lamb or slaughtered like a sheep, since he is invisible by nature.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Eustathius has just quoted Isaiah 53:2-3 about the servant's dishonored appearance, and now explains that these forms and sufferings attach to the man, not to the divine nature.

title: The man, not the indwelling God, suffered dishonor and death
english: Immediately the prophet brings in another quotation, adding: “A man in affliction, knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). So this is the one who was seen without appearance and without form after his insults, and then again through transformation was clothed with splendor. For the God dwelling in him was not led to death like a lamb or slaughtered like a sheep, since he is invisible by nature.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Eustathius has just quoted Isaiah 53:3 about a man in affliction and is now explaining that this man, not the God dwelling in him, is the one who suffered dishonor and then regained splendor.

title: The man of affliction is the one who later put on splendor; the indwelling God did not suffer
english: Immediately he brings in another quotation, adding: “A man in affliction, knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3). So this is the one who was seen without appearance and without form after his insults, and then again through transformation was clothed with splendor. For the God dwelling in him was not led to death like a lamb or slaughtered like a sheep, since he is invisible by nature.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Eustathius is closing his argument that the suffering described by Isaiah belongs to the man in whom God dwells, not to the divine nature.
